quote: Wann [-k-]kann die Kette abbrechen, so dass wir nichts neues[?]
english: When can the chain terminate, so that we [obtain] nothing new[?]
topic: A list of research notes: treating certain functions by analogy with Eisenstein's work on the p-function via infinite products, addition theorems for p and σ, turning covariant criteria into invariant ones, decomposition conditions for binary forms in several variables, vanishing of transvectants, Klein's topic of a typical representation of the Kummer surface, and termination of chains of transvection processes.

triage.modern_statement: This note is a fragment, so any reading of it is an interpretation. Its context on the page is 'termination of chains of transvection processes' in the classical invariant theory of binary forms. Read that way, Hilbert is asking: if you start from a set of ground forms and keep taking transvectants (Überschiebungen) of covariants already found, when does the process stop giving genuinely new covariants? Put another way, when are all further transvectants expressible as polynomials in the ones already found? That amounts to asking when, and with what bound, the algebra of covariants is finitely generated by the transvection procedure. This is the core of Gordan's finiteness algorithm and of the 'finite basis' problem for invariants and covariants.
triage.answered_by: For binary forms, Paul Gordan proved in 1868, constructively and with symbolic transvectant methods, that the covariants of any system of binary forms are finitely generated. Gordan's algorithm therefore terminates. In 1890 Hilbert himself proved the general finite basis theorem for forms of any degree in any number of variables, using a non-constructive approach. Constructive and degree-bound versions came later; modern work (e.g. Olive, arXiv 1403.2283) revisits the termination of Gordan's algorithm.

evidence.claim: Gordan proved the finiteness theorem for binary forms with symbolic methods. Hilbert proved the general finite basis theorem in 1890, which at first was criticized as non-constructive.

In 1868 Gordan proved that the covariants of any binary forms are always finitely generated. Hilbert's 1890 approach became the foundation of abstract invariant theory. Modern work re-examines Gordan's transvectant algorithm.

triage.why: The note is very short and only says 'Kette' (chain). The connection to transvection chains comes from the page summary, which lists 'termination of chains of transvection processes'. In that setting the natural question is when repeated transvection stops producing new covariants, which is exactly the finiteness and termination problem that Gordan settled for binary forms and Hilbert generalized in 1890. It is not one of the 23 problems as such (the 14th problem on finite generation is related but different). I can't tell from the text alone which specific chain, or what kind of stopping criterion, Hilbert meant. Computing explicit covariant bases and bounds is still studied, but the sources here don't establish that this question is an active research area in its own right.
